content: Puerperal fever, also known as childbed fever or puerperal sepsis, is a severe form of septicemia that can occur in women during or shortly after childbirth or abortion. Historically, its spread was often linked to unsanitary conditions. However, in modern medicine, it can still be caused by naturally occurring bacteria such as Group B Streptococcus (GBS, Streptococcus agalactiae), among others. The incidence of puerperal fever has significantly decreased due to improved hygiene practices during delivery and the use of antibiotics, which have greatly reduced associated mortality rates. In the 17th century, hospitals dedicated to childbirth, known as lying-in hospitals, became common in many European cities. These facilities, however, operated without knowledge of antisepsis. Patients were exposed to overcrowding, frequent vaginal examinations, and the use of contaminated instruments, dressings, and bedding. The first recorded epidemic of puerperal fever occurred at the Hôtel-Dieu de Paris in 1646. Throughout Europe and America, hospitals reported maternal death rates of 20–25% during childbirth, with intermittent epidemics resulting in nearly 100% fatality rates in some maternity wards. Several physicians began to suspect that contagion and poor hygiene were contributing factors in the spread of puerperal fever. In 1842, Thomas Watson, a Professor of Medicine at King’s College Hospital in London, emphasized the importance of handwashing and changing clothing for obstetric attendants to prevent the transmission of the disease. He recommended the use of chlorine solutions for handwashing to avoid practitioners becoming vectors of infection between patients. In 1843, Oliver Wendell Holmes published The Contagiousness of Puerperal Fever, controversially asserting that the disease was often transmitted from patient to patient by physicians and nurses. He advocated for handwashing, clean clothing, and the avoidance of autopsies by those assisting in childbirth as measures to prevent its spread. Holmes famously stated that he would prefer his loved ones to give birth unaided in a stable rather than risk exposure to the disease in a well-appointed hospital. His conclusions were met with ridicule by many contemporaries, including Charles Meigs, a prominent obstetrician, who dismissed the need for such measures, claiming that Doctors are gentlemen, and gentlemen’s hands are clean. In 1844, Ignaz Semmelweis was appointed assistant lecturer in the First Obstetric Division of the Vienna Hospital, where medical students were trained. Unaware of Holmes’ essay, Semmelweis observed that the mortality rate from puerperal fever in his division was 16%, significantly higher than the 2% rate in the Second Division, where midwifery students were trained. He also noted that puerperal fever was rare among women who gave birth before arriving at the hospital. Semmelweis discovered that doctors in the First Division performed autopsies on women who had died the previous day, whereas midwives were not required to do so. He made the connection between these autopsies and the spread of puerperal fever after a colleague, Jakob Kolletschka, died of septicemia following an accidental wound sustained during an autopsy. Semmelweis began experimenting with various cleansing agents and, in May 1847, mandated that all doctors and students in the First Division wash their hands with a chlorinated lime solution before starting ward work and before each vaginal examination. This intervention led to a dramatic reduction in the mortality rate from puerperal fever in the division, dropping from 18% in May 1847 to less than 3% by June–November of the same year. Despite these extraordinary results, Semmelweis faced skepticism and ridicule from his peers. The true mechanism of puerperal fever was not widely understood until the early 20th century. In 1879, Louis Pasteur demonstrated that streptococcus bacteria were present in the blood of women with puerperal fever. By the turn of the century, the importance of antiseptic techniques was widely accepted, and their implementation, along with the mid-20th-century introduction of new antibiotics, significantly reduced maternal mortality during childbirth. In modern times, puerperal fever remains rare but not eradicated. In 2004, a mother named Jessica Palmer died of puerperal fever caused by Group A Streptococcus in the UK. Her case received significant media attention, and her widower subsequently created a website to raise awareness about the disease, its symptoms, and its treatability.
